name: Victor Hansen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for seeing me. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say is confidential, so you can tell me the public answer and the private one. Can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Mornings I'm the class pianist at the Westbrook Ballet School, which means I play for the dance classes: the teacher calls out an exercise, says 'pliés, slow three', and I play something that fits. Then I sleep in the afternoon, and five nights a week I play the grand piano in the bar at the Carlton Hotel from seven till eleven. People ask for Sinatra, film themes, now and then something odd from a wedding. I'm still slow at improvising, so I lean on a big binder of arrangements, and the ballet teachers have to tell me twice sometimes.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Good, for a piano player. The Carlton pays a proper monthly fee and the tips at the weekend are decent. I lived with my parents till I was 25 and saved most of it, so I've got about nine months put by, and I rent a small flat on Mill Street on my own. I don't use any of the AI things. My phone's for calls and the bus times.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I say now: people at a hotel bar want a person at the piano, not a speaker. If it all turned out to be hype, I'd shrug and say most new things are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it'd mean nothing changes, and that suits me. My worries would be the normal ones, like the Carlton changing owners or the ballet school losing pupils. I'm not the best player around, so I keep my head down and turn up on time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep both jobs exactly as they are. I'd keep putting a few hundred a month into savings. Maybe I'd finally pay for some improvising lessons, because the binder only gets me so far.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine. Comfortable, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the Carlton changing owners. Has that been talked about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There was a rumour last spring that a hotel chain wanted to buy it. Nothing came of it. If it happened, the new people might want a cheaper player or none at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would any part of your day get automated in this world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The ballet school already has a speaker with recorded music for the little ones on Saturdays. That might spread a bit. But Mrs Lind (the ballet school's head teacher) likes a live pianist for the older classes, and she's the one who decides.

say: Hotel bar guests want **a person** at the piano, not a speaker.
Most new things turn out to be **hype**, so I'd shrug.
think: My real worries are the **Carlton** changing owners or the ballet school shrinking.
do: Keep both **jobs** exactly as they are now.
Put **a few hundred** a month into savings.
Pay for **improvising lessons** to rely less on the binder.
feel: **Comfortable**, because his routine would carry on.
S0.quote: Mrs Lind (the ballet school's head teacher) likes a live pianist for the older classes, and she's the one who decides.
fieldNote: His security rests on **two employers** and one teacher's taste.
He knows his **improvising** is weak and quietly plans to fix it.
His worries are about **ownership changes**, not technology.

steps.text: Keep playing ballet classes mornings and the Carlton bar five nights
Put a few hundred a month into savings
Pay for improvising lessons to rely less on his binder

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there are pros and cons, and live music will be fine. I wouldn't post anything, I don't really do that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the ballet job worries me more than the hotel. An app that listens to the ballet teacher and plays the right music is exactly the kind of thinking job AI takes over first. The Carlton bar is me sitting at a real piano, which is harder to replace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Mrs Lind directly if the school is looking at anything like that. I'd pick up an extra night or two at another hotel, the Regency on the river, as a backup. I wouldn't learn the apps; I'd put the time into learning more songs by heart.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. Not losing sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to your money if the ballet mornings go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd lose about a third of what I earn. With the savings and another hotel night I'd cover it, and I'd stop eating out after work as much. It wouldn't sink me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think should do something about this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bit of everyone. The companies should be honest about what their stuff does, and the government should make sure people get some notice. I don't think it's anyone's fault exactly, it's just how things move.

I don't really **post things**, so I'd keep it in person.
think: The **ballet job** is more at risk than the hotel bar.
An app that **listens to the teacher** could do my morning work.
do: Ask **Mrs Lind** directly if the school is looking at apps.
Pick up an **extra night** at the Regency hotel as a backup.
Learn **more songs** by heart instead of learning apps.
feel: **A bit uneasy**, but not losing sleep.
S1.quote: An app that listens to the ballet teacher and plays the right music is exactly the kind of thinking job AI takes over first.
fieldNote: He expects to keep his main income and could absorb losing **a third**.

His **centrist** view spreads responsibility without blaming anyone.

steps.text: Ask Mrs Lind whether the ballet school plans to use apps

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big shift and people should keep calm. I'd say the hotel still wants a pianist, because that's true for now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, by 2028 the ballet mornings are gone, I'm almost sure. The hotel bar lasts until the robots in 2031, and maybe a bit longer because guests like a real person. But I'd be a slow-improvising pianist with three years left in his main job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take every hotel night I can get across the city and save more than half of it. I'd ask the Carlton for a written contract, not a handshake. I'd cut back on things like the new suit I was going to buy, and stay in the flat on Mill Street rather than move somewhere nicer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It's like hearing the music's going to stop and not knowing when exactly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do the three years between 2028 and 2031 mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The three years before the robots are the last stretch where my hands still count. I'd want to be the best bar pianist in town by then, so if any hotel keeps one human, it's me. That's my only real plan, to be honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't use the apps. Would you change your mind here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I don't think so. I wouldn't know where to start, and it feels like helping the thing that's replacing me. Maybe that's daft.

say: It's a **big shift**, and people should keep calm.
The hotel **still wants a pianist**, which is true for now.
think: The **ballet mornings** are gone by 2028, I'm almost sure.
The hotel bar lasts only until the **robots in 2031**.
do: Take every **hotel night** possible and save more than half.
Ask the Carlton for a **written contract**.
Skip the **new suit** and stay in the Mill Street flat.
feel: **Anxious**, like knowing the music will stop without knowing when.
S2.quote: The three years before the robots are the last stretch where my hands still count.
fieldNote: He expects to lose a third of his income and his **main job** within five years.
His only plan is to be the **best bar pianist** left, which he admits is thin.
Refusing AI feels to him like not **helping the replacement**.

steps.text: Take every hotel bar night across the city and save half
Ask the Carlton Hotel for a written contract
Skip buying a new suit and stay in the Mill Street flat

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time to adjust, so nobody should panic. I'd tell the lads at the Carlton to get things in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd have the ballet job until about 2030 and the hotel until 2034 or so. That's a decent stretch. I'd use it to get much better at playing by ear, because a pianist who can play anything a guest hums lasts longest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd book weekly lessons with Anders, an old jazz pianist who plays at the Blue Door club, and work through his whole repertoire. I'd save hard but not cut much. I'd also ask a few weddings planners to put me on their lists, to spread my work around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, a bit. Less than the fast one, because I can see it coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said nobody should panic. Are you panicking?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. But I'm not as relaxed as I'd let on at work. If you'd asked me in a pub, I'd say it's fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first if money got tight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Taxis home after the late shift. I'd take the night bus instead. It's a small thing, but it adds up over a year.

say: **Five years** is time to adjust, so nobody should panic.
Colleagues at the Carlton should get things **in writing**.
think: The ballet job lasts to about **2030** and the hotel to about 2034.
A pianist who can **play anything** a guest hums lasts longest.
do: Book **weekly lessons** with Anders at the Blue Door club.
Get on **wedding planners'** lists to spread work around.
Save hard while cutting only **small comforts**.
feel: **Anxious**, but less than in the fast version because he can see it coming.
S3.quote: A pianist who can play anything a guest hums lasts longest.
fieldNote: He shows a clear **gap** between his calm public line and private worry.
His plan is all **craft**: playing by ear, not technology.
He spreads risk through **wedding work**, a cautious but real move.

steps.text: Book weekly lessons with Anders, a jazz pianist at the Blue Door club

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and lots of things could happen in between. That's what I'd say, and I'd mostly believe it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means I've got my whole thirties at the piano. By 2036 I'd be 37 and a decent player. The robots come around 2039, and by then I might have saved enough to do something else, though I don't know what.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am for the first year. Maybe start the improvising lessons. I'd keep saving and wait to see what the hotels actually do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's far off, so it doesn't feel real yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you don't know what you'd do after. Does that bother you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. My dad (a retired bus mechanic) always says have a second trade. I never listened. Maybe I should start thinking about it around 2030.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you move sooner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the Carlton let a pianist go anywhere in town, I'd move. Seeing it happen to someone I know would do it. Until then I'd just keep playing.

say: **Ten years** is a long time and lots could happen.
I'd say that at the Carlton and **mostly believe** it myself.
think: I've got my whole **thirties** at the piano.
By 2039 I might have **saved enough** to do something else.
do: Carry on **as I am** for the first year.
Start the **improvising lessons** at some point.
Keep **saving** and watch what the hotels do.
feel: **Uneasy**, but it doesn't feel real yet.
S4.quote: My dad (a retired bus mechanic) always says have a second trade. I never listened.
fieldNote: With a decade, he defaults to **waiting**, true to his resistant style.
His father's advice about a **second trade** nags at him.
He'd only move if he **saw a colleague** lose work first.

steps.text: Carry on with ballet mornings and Carlton evenings
Wait to see whether any hotel replaces a pianist
Keep saving part of each month's Carlton fee

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because the ballet job and then the hotel go too quickly for someone like me to learn something new. What would help is a decent notice period by law, so a hotel can't just replace you overnight, and some help paying for training in a second trade.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe whether people will still want to sit in a bar and listen to a real person. I think they will, for a while. Guests stand next to the piano at the Carlton Hotel and tell me about their wedding song, and nobody does that to a speaker.

He expects the **ballet mornings** to go first and the hotel bar to last until robots.
His public line is **calm**, but privately he admits a growing worry.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because both jobs go too fast for him to learn something new.
